description: We are a group of software and aerospace engineers, we compromise of both students and start-ups members.
summary:
Before anything goes to the Moon, someone has to test it on Earth, and the hard part is choosing where. ExplorerX is an interactive map of 20 top curated sites around the world that resemble the lunar surface in one way or another. For each site it calculates a Planetary Match Index from five factors: terrain slope and roughness, thermal extremes and temperature, aridity and anhydrous soil, mineral and silicate match, and volcanic or basaltic geology.
The sliders are the part we care about most. A rover team needs rough terrain, a cold-survival test needs big temperature swings, and a drilling test needs the right bedrock, so each team sets its own priorities and the rankings and site dossiers update straight away. Click a site and a real-time 3D terrain view opens, with the steepness of the relief driven by that site's terrain score. We built Terrestrial Lunar Analog Finder for the NASA Space Apps Challenge as a way to match Earth locations to lunar landing sites such as Shackleton Crater. The goal is to give researchers, mission planners, and engineers a transparent way to pick a test site for lunar rovers, surface habitats, and life-support protocols, and to inform future landing site choices.
details:
Project Details

Space agencies do not send a rover or habitat to the Moon without testing it somewhere harsh on Earth first. Picking that test site usually means digging through scattered papers and datasets, so we put the comparison in one place.

ExplorerX has three parts: the map and dossiers, a 3D terrain view, and the data behind it.

  • The map and dossiers: A global map of 20 top analog sites sits next to a live leaderboard. At the default weights, Anatolia is first at 75.9%. Five sliders control how much each factor weighs. The defaults are Terrain 25%, Thermal 25%, Aridity 20%, Composition 15%, and Geology 15%, and you can change them to fit your test. Click any site and you get its Site Dossier: exact coordinates, the distance to the nearest logistics hub/city, a bar with percentage for each of the five factors, a Mission Suitability Verdict, and limitations under a section called Where the Analogy Breaks Down. No Earth site is a perfect Moon, so the tool says where each one falls short as well as where it fits. It also flags unsuitable zones, where human interference or water coverage rules out analog testing.

Figure 1: The global map with the ranked leaderboard of top lunar analogs.

Figure 2: The five priority sliders for Terrain, Thermal, Aridity, Composition, and Geology.

Moving a slider updates every score in real time using this weighted formula:

Lunar Match % = [(S_Terrain * W_1 + S_Thermal * W_2 + S_Aridity * W_3 + S_Composition * W_4 + S_Geology * W_5) / (W_1 + W_2 + W_3 + W_4 + W_5)] * 100

Figure 3: The Site Dossier for Great Basin (California), ranked #02, with its coordinates, the nearest logistics hub (Bishop, 130 km), and a Planetary Match Index of 75.7%.

Figure 4: The five factor scores for the same site, its Mission Suitability Verdict, and its note on where the analogy breaks down.

  • The 3D terrain view: Click a site and ExplorerX opens a real-time 3D topographic slope simulation of its terrain, so engineers can inspect relative relief next to real orbital satellite imagery. The ridge shape is generated from the site's own coordinates (for example 39.6250°, 44.1250° for Anatolia), which act as a unique seed, so no two sites share the same ridge shape. The steepness of the peaks is scaled directly from that site's terrain score. The 2D map behind the 3D view shows the Esri orbital satellite photograph of that exact spot. The view shows relative steepness, not a measured elevation profile.
  • The data pipeline: where the numbers come from. We pulled multi-year Earth observation data for every candidate site: elevation and slope (ETOPO 2022), land surface temperature and vegetation (MODIS), humidity, precipitation, and soil moisture (MERRA-2), and bedrock type (GLiM). Each measurement was compared against a lunar benchmark (LRO Diviner for temperature, LRO LOLA for topography, and Apollo and Luna 24 RELAB spectra for minerals) and turned into a 0 to 100% similarity score. We also added the nearest town to each site (Natural Earth) plus short engineering notes. All of that is worked out ahead of time, so when you move a slider the app only reweights the five stored sub-scores for each site and re-ranks them instantly.
  • How the frontend is built: We built a fast, lightweight web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, paired with Leaflet.js and Esri World Imagery to display our 20 locations on an interactive world map. For the interactive 3D terrain view, we used Three.js to render a 360-degree rotatable 3D terrain model shaped by each site's real slope data. Client-side JavaScript calculates the slider weights and re-ranks sites instantaneously in the browser without needing a heavy backend server, and the application is hosted live on Netlify.
